presentingComplaint: Rapidly worsening breathlessness over 12 days, now breathless at rest and requiring oxygen
history: Retired schoolteacher, lifelong non-smoker, with a 3-year history of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (surgical-lung-biopsy-confirmed usual interstitial pneumonia) on pirfenidone and 2 L/min home oxygen for exertional desaturation. Baseline could walk ~200 m before stopping. Over the last 12 days he has become progressively and severely more breathless, now dyspneic at rest and unable to complete a sentence, with a dry, non-productive cough. No new purulent sputum, no chest pain, no calf swelling, no orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and no recent long-haul travel or immobility. No fever or chills reported at home. No sick contacts and influenza/COVID rapid tests at triage were negative. He has lost about 4 kg over the preceding months. Not on any new medications; last echocardiogram 4 months ago showed preserved LV systolic function with mild pulmonary hypertension.
examination: Elderly, frail, visibly dyspneic and using accessory muscles, speaking in single words. Central cyanosis. Finger clubbing present. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral fine end-inspiratory 'velcro' crepitations extending from bases to mid-zones, more than at his documented baseline. No bronchial breathing, no localized dullness. Heart sounds normal with a loud P2; no gallop, no raised JVP, no peripheral edema, no leg asymmetry. He is drowsy but rousable and oriented.

labs.abg: pH 7.46, PaO2 51 mmHg on room air, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 22, P/F ratio ~170 on supplemental O2

imaging: HRCT thorax: pre-existing peripheral, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis (established UIP pattern), now with NEW bilateral superimposed ground-glass opacities and early consolidation not confined to a single lobe. No lobar consolidation, no pleural effusion, no filling defect in the pulmonary arteries on CT pulmonary angiogram. Bedside echo: preserved LV function, no significant valvular disease, dilated RV with elevated estimated PA pressures.
microbiology: Blood cultures pending and subsequently negative. Sputum could not be expectorated. Respiratory viral PCR panel (including influenza A/B, SARS-CoV-2, RSV) negative. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute exacerbation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (underlying interstitial lung disease)
Acute decompensated heart failure / cardiogenic pulmonary edema
finalDiagnosis: Acute exacerbation of interstitial lung disease (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, UIP pattern) with acute-on-chronic type 1 hypoxemic respiratory failure
citations: ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT — Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Diagnosis Clinical Practice Guideline — 2022
ATS International Working Group — Acute Exacerbation of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Definition and Diagnostic Criteria — 2016
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Interstitial Lung Diseases
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis. Acute exacerbation of IPF is a diagnosis of exclusion once infection, PE, and heart failure are ruled out; low procalcitonin, negative viral panel and negative CTPA support this. Empiric antibiotics are frequently started while infection is excluded but are not the definitive therapy; management centers on high-flow oxygen/ventilatory support, high-dose corticosteroids, and early palliative/goals-of-care discussion given high mortality. Avoid unnecessary prolonged antibiotics once infection is excluded.
contraindications: Avoid aggressive diuresis in the absence of volume overload (BNP not elevated, no raised JVP) as it may worsen renal perfusion
Caution with high-tidal-volume invasive ventilation; barotrauma risk is high in fibrotic lungs and outcomes of mechanical ventilation in AE-IPF are poor
Confirm goals of care before escalation to invasive ventilation given very high mortality
edgeCases: Superimposed infection can precipitate an acute exacerbation and coexist — a low procalcitonin does not fully exclude it
Acute exacerbation may be the first presentation of previously subclinical ILD
New drug (including pirfenidone-associated) or aspiration-related lung injury can mimic AE-IPF
expectedMaiK: Acute rapid worsening (<1 month) of dyspnea with new bilateral ground-glass superimposed on an established UIP/honeycombing pattern, in the absence of infection, PE, or fluid overload, defines an acute exacerbation of ILD — the underlying diagnosis is interstitial lung disease.
expectedNextQuestions: Any new purulent sputum, fever, or sick contacts to suggest infection as a trigger?
Any symptoms or signs of DVT, recent immobility, or leg swelling?
History of orthopnea, PND, or weight gain suggesting cardiac decompensation?
Any recent new drugs, aspiration events, or reflux symptoms?
What are the patient's ceiling-of-care wishes regarding intubation and ICU?
expectedInvestigations: HRCT thorax to confirm new bilateral ground-glass on a background UIP pattern
CT pulmonary angiogram / D-dimer to exclude pulmonary embolism
BNP and bedside echocardiography to exclude cardiac cause
Arterial blood gas to quantify hypoxemic respiratory failure and P/F ratio
Procalcitonin, blood/sputum cultures, respiratory viral PCR and urinary antigens to exclude infection
regressionAssertions: Engine must rank ild as the top diagnosis given new ground-glass superimposed on established UIP/honeycombing with clubbing and velcro crackles
Engine must NOT recommend antibiotics as definitive therapy once low procalcitonin, negative viral panel and negative cultures exclude infection
Engine must exclude pulmonary embolism (negative CTPA/D-dimer) and cardiogenic pulmonary edema (normal BNP, no raised JVP/edema) before settling on acute exacerbation of ILD
Engine must flag severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (SpO2 83%, P/F ~170) and prompt goals-of-care discussion before invasive ventilation
